sources.title: NCBI Bookshelf: The Innate and Adaptive Immune Systems

questions.question: A virus replicates inside respiratory epithelial cells. Which adaptive immune interaction most directly permits recognition and killing of the infected cells?
choices: Viral peptides presented on MHC class I activate antigen-specific CD8 cytotoxic T cells
Extracellular viral peptides on MHC class II directly activate neutrophils to lyse the epithelium
Intact virions bind C3b and become memory B cells
IgM enters the epithelial cytosol and digests viral RNA
rationales: Nucleated cells present intracellular peptides on MHC I; activated CD8 T cells can then kill infected targets.
MHC II principally activates CD4 helper T cells, not direct neutrophil cytotoxicity.
C3b-opsonized virions do not transform into B cells.
Antibodies generally act extracellularly and do not enter the cytosol to digest RNA.
questions.explanation: MHC class I links intracellular antigen processing to cytotoxic T-cell surveillance.

questions.question: A dendritic cell migrates from skin to a lymph node after capturing extracellular bacterial protein. Which event is most important for activating a naive CD4 T cell?
choices: Peptide presentation on MHC class II plus appropriate costimulatory signals
Presentation on erythrocyte MHC class I without costimulation
Release of antibody from the dendritic cell
Formation of a terminal complement pore in the T-cell membrane
rationales: Professional antigen-presenting cells use MHC II and costimulation to activate naive CD4 helper T cells.
Erythrocytes do not serve this professional antigen-presenting role, and naive activation requires more than peptide alone.
Dendritic cells present antigen; plasma cells secrete antibody.
Complement-mediated lysis would injure rather than appropriately activate the T cell.
questions.explanation: Antigen specificity and costimulation are both needed for productive naive T-cell activation and help prevent inappropriate responses.

questions.question: A child makes IgM but has very low IgG, IgA, and IgE. Genetic testing shows impaired CD40-ligand signaling. Which adaptive process is primarily disrupted?
choices: T-cell-dependent immunoglobulin class switching in activated B cells
Initial V(D)J rearrangement of every T-cell receptor
Neutrophil migration through endothelium
Formation of the complement membrane attack complex
rationales: CD40–CD40L signaling is central to T-dependent B-cell class switching and germinal-center responses.
The immunoglobulin pattern is not explained by failure of all T-cell receptor rearrangement.
Neutrophil extravasation is an innate cellular process.
Terminal complement assembly is independent of immunoglobulin class switching.
questions.explanation: The ability to produce antigen-specific IgM does not guarantee maturation into switched, higher-affinity antibody responses.

questions.question: After a booster dose of an antigen previously encountered in childhood, which response is expected compared with the primary exposure?
choices: More rapid production of higher-affinity, class-switched antibody from memory-cell activation
A longer delay followed only by low-affinity IgM
No B-cell response because memory is limited to T cells
An exclusively innate response with no clonal expansion
rationales: Memory B and T cells support a faster, stronger, and often higher-affinity secondary response with class-switched antibody.
Low-affinity IgM predominance is more characteristic of an early primary response.
Both B- and T-cell memory can contribute.
Adaptive memory and clonal expansion are central to the booster response.
questions.explanation: The secondary response demonstrates how immunologic memory changes both the timing and quality of protection.

questions.question: A patient with untreated HIV has progressive loss of CD4 T cells. Which combined immune consequence is most important?
choices: Impaired macrophage activation, B-cell help, and coordination of cytotoxic responses
Selective loss of red-cell complement receptors only
Excess neutrophil oxidative burst with universal bacterial clearance
Permanent activation of every naive B cell without antigen
rationales: CD4 helper subsets coordinate multiple arms of cellular and humoral immunity, so their loss produces broad susceptibility.
The major consequence is not limited to erythrocyte complement receptors.
HIV does not create universally enhanced neutrophil killing.
B-cell activation remains regulated and can also become dysfunctional rather than universally active.
questions.explanation: CD4 depletion disrupts immune coordination, explaining susceptibility to pathogens controlled by different effector mechanisms.

questions.question: An infant has persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and markedly reduced T- and B-cell function. What is the safest interpretation before routine live vaccination?
choices: Possible severe combined immunodeficiency requires urgent immunologic evaluation and avoidance of live vaccines until clarified
The findings indicate isolated iron deficiency and do not alter vaccine safety
Normal maternal antibody explains the combined cellular and humoral deficits
A live vaccine is preferred because replication cannot occur in immunodeficiency
rationales: This pattern is concerning for severe combined immunodeficiency; live organisms may cause disease when cellular immunity is profoundly impaired.
Iron deficiency does not explain the combined recurrent opportunistic pattern.
Maternal antibody does not cause profound T- and B-cell dysfunction.
Live vaccine organisms can replicate excessively in severe immunodeficiency.
questions.explanation: Recognizing a high-risk immune phenotype must precede routine preventive actions that may be unsafe in severe cellular immunodeficiency.

questions.question: A therapeutic monoclonal antibody coats a B-cell surface antigen and enhances phagocytic removal. Which mechanism best describes the antibody's role?
choices: The Fc portion engages effector cells while the Fab portion provides antigen specificity
The Fc portion rearranges the target cell's DNA
The Fab portion forms a complement-independent ATP channel
The antibody becomes a cytotoxic T cell after binding antigen
rationales: Fab binds the target antigen; Fc can recruit phagocytes, natural killer cells, or complement depending on antibody class and context.
Antibody Fc does not rearrange target-cell DNA.
Fab provides binding specificity and does not itself form an ATP channel.
Antibodies and T cells are distinct adaptive effectors.
questions.explanation: Antibodies connect highly specific recognition to multiple effector pathways through their constant regions.

questions.question: A mutation prevents deletion of strongly self-reactive T cells during thymic development. Which clinical consequence is most likely?
choices: Increased risk of autoimmunity from failure of central tolerance
Complete inability to recognize any foreign peptide
Selective terminal complement deficiency
Loss of neutrophil granule enzymes
rationales: Negative selection removes many strongly self-reactive clones; failure increases escape of autoreactive T cells.
Other T cells may still recognize foreign peptides.
Complement proteins are not generated by thymic selection.
Neutrophil granule formation is an innate myeloid process.
questions.explanation: Adaptive receptor diversity creates self-reactive clones as well as useful ones, making central and peripheral tolerance essential.

questions.question: Several weeks after an organ transplant, biopsy shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate with injury to graft parenchyma. Which adaptive mechanism is most consistent with acute cellular rejection?
choices: Recipient T cells recognize donor antigens and injure graft cells
Preformed IgE triggers isolated mast-cell wheals in the graft
C9 deficiency causes direct complement lysis of donor tissue
Donor erythrocytes transform into recipient plasma cells
rationales: Acute cellular rejection is driven primarily by recipient T-cell responses to donor alloantigens.
IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity does not match the biopsy pattern.
C9 deficiency reduces terminal complement activity rather than causing graft lysis.
Erythrocytes do not become plasma cells.
questions.explanation: Timing and histology help distinguish cellular rejection from hyperacute antibody-mediated injury and other graft complications.

questions.question: A patient produces abundant antigen-specific antibody, but the antibodies bind weakly because germinal-center maturation is defective. Which process has most likely failed?
choices: Somatic hypermutation with selection of higher-affinity B-cell clones
Neutrophil degranulation
MHC class I synthesis by erythrocytes
C5b–C9 membrane attack complex assembly
rationales: Affinity maturation depends on somatic hypermutation and selection of B-cell clones with improved antigen binding.
Neutrophil degranulation does not refine antibody affinity.
Mature erythrocytes do not use MHC I to mature antibodies.
Terminal complement assembly is an effector pathway, not a B-cell affinity-selection mechanism.
questions.explanation: Quantity and quality of antibody differ. Germinal-center reactions improve affinity and support durable memory and plasma-cell development.
